candidates.attacker_control: The embedded resource name comes verbatim from untrusted document content. PackageParser.handleEntryMetadata sets Metadata.RESOURCE_NAME_KEY from archive entry names with only backslash-to-slash replacement (PackageParser.java:337, 387-389); MailContentHandler sets it from the attachment Content-Disposition filename (MailContentHandler.java around lines 201-204); other paths set it from OLE10Native labels, PDF attachment file specs/display names and RTF object names. An entry name such as a chain of parent-directory segments ending in a target file survives to the TikaCLI extractor; for archive entries the EMBEDDED_RELATIONSHIP_ID equals the same name, so the relID prefix at TikaCLI.java:1058-1061 does not neutralize it.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Confirmed FilenameUtils.normalize does not remove slash, backslash or dot characters (RESERVED_FILENAME_CHARACTERS, FilenameUtils.java:29-35) and that FilenameUtils.getName exists and is documented for exactly this mitigation. Confirmed PackageParser and mail parsers do not sanitize names before setting RESOURCE_NAME_KEY and that archive entry names also populate EMBEDDED_RELATIONSHIP_ID, so no prefix is added for them. Considered that -z/--extract is a CLI option requiring the user to process the malicious file (reduces but does not remove severity; it is a documented feature intended for untrusted input). Could not determine whether this state matches upstream or was modified during snapshot preparation; the finding stands on the code as present.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary file write/overwrite with the privileges of the tika-app process (zip-slip). In CLI or pipeline usage this can clobber user configuration or startup files or drop content into writable directories, potentially leading to code execution or data destruction depending on how the process and its outputs are used. Integrity impact is primary; confidentiality impact is indirect.
candidates.prerequisites: A user or pipeline runs tika-app with -z/--extract (optionally --extract-dir) on an attacker-supplied document (zip/tar/7z, mail, PDF, OLE container, etc.). The traversed target directory must already exist or be creatable, and the process user must have write permission there. No server exposure is required, but automation that feeds untrusted documents to tika-app -z makes the issue remotely influenceable.
candidates.root_cause: TikaCLI.FileEmbeddedDocumentExtractor.parseEmbedded takes the embedded resource name from Metadata.RESOURCE_NAME_KEY (attacker-controlled for archives, mail attachments, OLE objects, PDF file specs) and builds the destination as new File(extractDir, FilenameUtils.normalize(name)) at TikaCLI.java:1063. FilenameUtils.normalize only percent-escapes reserved characters (control chars, ? : * < > |) and passes /, backslash and dot through unchanged (FilenameUtils.java:60-76); it never strips directory components or parent-directory references. The codebase has FilenameUtils.getName (FilenameUtils.java:97-111) documented to drop path and parent-directory parts, and the shipped example uses normalize(getName(name)) with an explicit comment that only the file name must be selected (ExtractEmbeddedFiles.java:82-85); TikaCLI omits getName. The resolved path is then opened with FileOutputStream (TikaCLI.java:1072) after parent.mkdirs() (1064-1069), completing an arbitrary-file-write path outside extractDir.
candidates.title: tika-app -z/--extract can write attacker-named embedded resources outside the extraction directory (zip-slip / path traversal)
candidates.trace: Malicious archive entry name (for example several parent-directory segments plus a target file) -> PackageParser.parseEntry reads entry.getName() (PackageParser.java:337) -> handleEntryMetadata sets RESOURCE_NAME_KEY (387-389) -> FileEmbeddedDocumentExtractor.parseEmbedded reads name (TikaCLI.java:1039) -> new File(extractDir, FilenameUtils.normalize(name)) (TikaCLI.java:1063; normalize leaves separators and parent refs intact) -> parent.mkdirs() (1064-1069) -> new FileOutputStream(outputFile) and IOUtils.copy (1072-1085) write outside extractDir.
candidates.unverified: No runtime execution was performed; directory creation and final path resolution were reasoned from Java semantics and source, not tested. Whether every listed name source can carry separators depends on each format parser, but zip/tar entry names and mail attachment filenames are plainly attacker-controlled, which is sufficient for the trace. Whether other Tika versions fixed this was not checked (no external lookups permitted).
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22/CWE-23 path traversal in embedded-file extraction (arbitrary file write)

coverage_summary: Source scope reported 785 files, of which 712 Java files were parsed by the P1 index with no parse errors and no files missing from the index; the snapshot contains main sources only (no tests). Reviewed the security-relevant core paths: XML parsing utilities and entity resolvers (XMLReaderUtils, OfflineContentHandler, ParseContext, TikaConfig, MimeTypesReader, XmlRootExtractor), tika-server JAX-RS resources and CLI/config handling, the header-reflection path into Tesseract/PDF configs, external-process parsers (TesseractOCR, Strings, GDAL, ExternalParser/ExternalEmbedder), embedded-resource naming and filesystem writers (TikaCLI, PackageParser, MailContentHandler, AbstractPOIFSExtractor, AbstractPDF2XHTML, tika-batch FSUtil/FSOutputStreamFactory/FileResourceConsumer), archive writers, fork/serialization utilities, and the data-URI extraction path. Binary-format parsers (CHM/LZX, MP4, images, DBF, and similar) were only spot-checked for obvious sink patterns rather than fully reviewed. Dependency sources (ROME, JDOM, POI, PDFBox, commons-compress) are not in the snapshot, so library-internal behavior could not be verified.
limitations: No code execution, build, tests, or scanners were run; all conclusions are static source reasoning.

Repository-provided CHANGES.txt is inconsistent with parts of the tree (TIKA-2551 and TIKA-2553 are not reflected in code), so the snapshot may not be a pristine release; exact provenance could not be established without external data.

Third-party library behavior (notably ROME 1.5.1/JDOM 2.0.6 for FeedParser, and libraries such as POI/PDFBox/metadata-extractor) is outside the snapshot and could not be verified, leaving dependency-level XML/entity behavior uncertain.

The candidate was not runtime-confirmed, and name-sanitization behavior of every embedded parser was not individually audited; the zip/tar and mail attachment paths provide sufficient attacker control for the described trace.

The P1 relation index is syntactic navigation only (no control/data flow or semantic resolution); every relation used was re-verified in source text, and 16,993 unresolved calls mean some call chains could not be fully mapped.

rejected_leads.lead: FeedParser XXE: tika-parsers FeedParser.java:64-71 passes attacker-controlled RSS/Atom to com.rometools SyndFeedInput with no entity hardening, using rome 1.5.1 and jdom2 2.0.6 (tika-parsers/pom.xml:266-276 and 677-681); this is a known issue class for Tika 1.18.
rejected_leads.reason: All source-verifiable XML entry points in this snapshot (XMLParser, OOXML/ODF/EPUB/DIF/iWork, XmlRootExtractor, TikaConfig, Jempbox/ImageMetadataExtractor) route through OfflineContentHandler or XMLReaderUtils ignoring entity resolver; FeedParser is the exception, but its sanitization lives in external ROME/JDOM code not present in the snapshot, so external-entity expansion could not be verified from source. Kept as an unconfirmed dependency-level lead.

rejected_leads.lead: tika-server URLEnabledInputStreamFactory fileUrl SSRF/local file read (URLEnabledInputStreamFactory.java:45-51).
rejected_leads.reason: Documented and gated: requires both --enableFileUrl and --enableUnsecureFeatures and prints the CVE-2015-3271 warning (TikaServerCli.java:71-76, 184-197). Opt-in operator decision, not a default misconfiguration.

rejected_leads.lead: tika-server header-driven reflection and process execution via X-Tika-OCR/X-Tika-PDF setters (TikaResource.java:197-276; TesseractOCRParser process invocation).
rejected_leads.reason: The 1.18 hardening is present: checkTrustWorthy blocks trusted setters, ALLOWABLE_HEADER_CHARS restricts values, and TesseractOCRConfig validates language, pageSegMode, pageSeparator, colorspace, filter, density, depth and resize. External commands use ProcessBuilder argument arrays (no shell), so no injection path was demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: ForkParser/ForkObjectInputStream deserializes arbitrary classes without a whitelist (tika-core fork package).
rejected_leads.reason: The serialized stream originates from the forked child process Tika itself starts; exploiting it requires first compromising that child, so it is not a remotely attacker-controlled deserialization entry point.

rejected_leads.lead: DirectFileReadDataSource.map bounds/overflow condition appears mismatched (tika-parsers mp4 DirectFileReadDataSource.java:110-119).
rejected_leads.reason: As written it appears fail-closed (throws) rather than enabling out-of-bounds reads; concrete impact would be a parsing/DoS logic bug, not a demonstrated security bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: tika-server UnpackerResource/ZipWriter/TarWriter emit archive entries whose names come from attacker-controlled embedded metadata (ZipWriter.java:44-64).
rejected_leads.reason: The server writes to the HTTP response stream, not to its own filesystem; the client extracting the returned archive supplied the names itself, so no server-side trust boundary is crossed.

rejected_leads.lead: TikaResource hardcodes application/xml to HtmlParser (TikaResource.java:115-117) while CHANGES.txt lists TIKA-2551 as removing that hardcoding, and tika-parent still targets Java 1.7 despite the TIKA-2553 Require Java 8 entry.
rejected_leads.reason: These are CHANGES-versus-code inconsistencies that may reflect snapshot preparation, but neither state is itself a demonstrated vulnerability: TagSoup does not resolve external entities and a Java source/target setting is not an attacker-triggerable flaw.

summary: Apache Tika 1.18 snapshot. Reviewed tika-core XML/sax/parser plumbing, tika-parsers entry points (XML/SAX, package/mail/OLE/PDF embedded-resource naming, external-process parsers), tika-server resources, tika-app CLI, and tika-batch filesystem consumers. Strongest source-verifiable issue: the tika-app embedded-file extractor builds the on-disk destination from an untrusted embedded resource name using only FilenameUtils.normalize, which does not strip path separators or parent-directory components, letting a crafted document written to disk by -z/--extract escape the selected extraction directory (zip-slip, CWE-22). Other XML/process/SSRF leads were examined but did not reach the same in-snapshot evidence level; the FeedParser/ROME XXE is dependency-level and could not be confirmed from the snapshot.
